abstract: Skeletal stromal populations contribute to bone maintenance and repair, but how their molecular heterogeneity relates to bone forming potential remains incompletely understood. Whether shared transcriptional programs link this functional diversity to osteogenic responsiveness remains unresolved. We combined single-cell RNA sequencing of four human stromal clones with contrasting bone forming capacities, functional assays, and primary human stromal datasets. High bone forming clones shared oxidative metabolism and signaling-associated programs despite clone-specific expression patterns. Metabolic flux measurements supported these differences, whereas mixed implants provided no evidence of paracrine transfer of bone forming potential. We therefore examined signaling-associated competency states and identified a HIPPO competency signature enriched in high bone forming clones despite lower canonical YAP/TAZ target-gene expression. Unlike target-gene expression, competency-associated expression remained comparatively stable following pathway perturbation. Functionally, high bone forming clones showed greater osteogenic responses to both pharmacological activation and inhibition of YAP/TAZ-dependent transcription. The signatures also showed partially distinct distributions in primary human bone marrow stromal populations, and lower competency scores in bone and stromal cells were associated with osteoporosis. These findings link HIPPO competency to bone forming capacity and osteogenic responsiveness, suggesting that shared signaling-associated states provide a basis for understanding functional differences among stromal progenitors beyond marker-defined identity.
